ranges.en: Mishna's general rule listing those exempt from Festival appearance, ending with the one unable to ascend to Jerusalem.
Schools dispute the minor's threshold: whether he must ride on his father's shoulders or merely hold his hand.
Beit Hillel ground their position in the verse about three regalim, reading the term as referring to feet.
Beit Shammai's valuation: appearance offering worth two silver coins, peace offering one ma'a.
Beit Hillel's reversed valuation: appearance offering one ma'a, peace offering two silver coins.
Gemara asks what the word 'all' in the mishna is meant to add to the obligation.
Answer: it includes a person who is half slave and half free.
Raises Ravina's view that a half-slave is exempt, and asks again what 'all' adds, proposing a lame person case.
Answer: someone lame on the first festival day who was healed on the second day.
Challenges this answer: it works only if all festival days are equal, not if the first day is primary.
Asks again what 'all' adds, now under the view that the first day is primary.
Answer: it adds a person blind in one eye.
Rejects this answer as inconsistent with a different tanna's view.
Brings a baraita of Yohanan ben Dehavai citing Rabbi Yehuda: one blind in one eye is exempt, citing the verse.
Derives the exemption from the verse's wording: just as seeing uses both eyes, being seen requires both eyes.
Alternative answer: the mishna does include the half-slave, as stated at the outset.
Defends Ravina: the apparent conflict with his position is not a real difficulty.
Explains the discrepancy: this mishna follows its first version, while Ravina follows the final version.
Cites a mishna about one who is half slave and half free, to support the discussion.
That mishna rules the half-slave works for his master one day and for himself the next.
Attributes to Beit Hillel the ruling that the half-slave divides his days between master and self.
Beit Shammai objects to Beit Hillel's ruling; the passage breaks off at the end of the daf.

ranges.en: Objects that the ruling fixes the master's situation but leaves the half-slave unable to marry either a maidservant or a free woman.
Objects that idleness is not an option, since the world was created for procreation.
Cites Isaiah's verse that God did not create the world a waste but formed it to be inhabited.
Replies that the ruling is made for the betterment of the world, not for the man's own benefit.
Upholds the ruling: the master is compelled to free him and the slave owes his master half his value.
Reports that Beit Hillel retracted and ruled in accordance with Beit Shammai's view.
Quotes the mishna's exception clause listing the deaf-mute, imbecile and minor.
Explains what the mishna teaches by grouping the deaf-mute with the imbecile and minor.
Cites a mishna in Terumot: the ḥeresh is one who neither hears nor speaks; one who only speaks or only hears is obligated.
Brings a Tosefta that classifies the one who speaks without hearing as deaf, and the reverse as mute.
Asks from where the derivation comes that one who speaks without hearing is a deaf person and the reverse a mute.
Cites Psalms 38:14, 'I am as a deaf man, I hear not; and as a dumb man who does not open his mouth.'
Alternative answer: the word illem is an acronym for a phrase meaning his speech has been taken.
States the Tosefta's ruling that one who speaks without hearing, or hears without speaking, is obligated in mitzvot.
Objects that a baraita rules such a person is exempt, contradicting the Tosefta.
Resolves the contradiction: the mishna is incomplete and should read the clause about rejoicing.
Reconstructed mishna: all obligated in appearance and rejoicing, except the deaf-mute exempt from appearance but not rejoicing, and others exempt from both.
Cites a baraita with the same ruling, supporting the reconstructed version of the mishna.

ranges.en: Restates the ruling that the deaf-mute, imbecile and minor are exempt from rejoicing as well, since they are exempt from all Torah mitzvot.
Asks what distinguishes these groups: why are they exempt from appearance yet obligated in rejoicing?
Explains that exemption from appearance is derived by verbal analogy from the mitzva of assembly, citing Deuteronomy 31.
Asks where the assembly exemption of the deaf and mute comes from, and cites a baraita reading 'that they may hear' and 'learn'.
Asks whether the verse implies that one who cannot speak cannot learn at all.
Relates the incident of two mute nephews of a sage who nodded and moved their lips while attending study hall.
Reports that after prayer they were healed and proved proficient in Mishna, Sifra, Sifrei and the Talmud, showing mutes can learn.
Mar Zutra reads the verse as 'yelamdu' (that they may teach), so a mute may learn but not teach others.
Rav Ashi rejects reading 'yilmedu' (that they may learn) because it would wrongly imply the mute cannot learn.
States the implication of the rejected reading: if speech and hearing are needed for learning, the verse would be redundant.
Concludes the verse must read 'yelamdu', since the exemption cannot be derived from 'yishme'u' and the verse teaches teaching.
Rabbi Tanḥum rules that one deaf in one ear is exempt from the mitzva of appearance.
Cites Deuteronomy 31:11 'in their ears' as the basis for that ruling.
Asks why 'in their ears' is needed, since it could be used to teach that Torah must enter all Israelites' ears.
Answers that the requirement for the entire people is derived from 'before all Israel' instead.
Objects that if 'before all Israel' alone taught it, the text would not require hearing, so 'in their ears' is needed.
Replies that the need to hear is derived from 'that they may hear', leaving 'in their ears' to teach the one-ear ruling.
Rabbi Tanḥum rules that one lame in one leg is exempt from the mitzva of appearance.
Cites Exodus 23:14 'regalim' (feet) as the basis for requiring two usable legs.
Asks why 'regalim' is needed, since it would otherwise exclude people with artificial legs.
Answers that the exclusion of artificial legs is derived from 'pe'amim' in Exodus 23:17.
Cites a baraita and verses from Isaiah and Song of Songs showing that 'pe'amim' means legs.
Rava's homiletic reading: the feet of Israel are praised when ascending on the Festival, and 'prince' refers to Abraham.
Asks why the verse names the God of Abraham alone and not also Isaac and Jacob.
Answers that Abraham is named because he was the first to bring converts under God's name.
Reports a teaching of Rabbi Tanḥum, transmitted through Rav Kahana and Rav Natan bar Manyumi.
Asks what the verse about the empty pit means, since an empty pit obviously has no water.
Explains that the verse means the pit had no water but was full of snakes and scorpions.
Introduces a tannaitic story of Rabbi Yoḥanan ben Beroka and Rabbi Elazar ben Ḥisma visiting Rabbi Yehoshua.
Rabbi Yehoshua asks what novel teaching was delivered in the study hall that day.
The students reply that they are his disciples and drink from his teaching, so they have nothing new to offer.
Rabbi Yehoshua rejects that excuse: a study hall cannot exist without some novelty.
Asks whose week of lecturing it was that day.
Answers that it was the week of Rabbi Elazar ben Azarya.
Asks what subject was lectured on that day.
Answers that the lecture concerned the portion on the assembly.
Asks what homiletic interpretation was given of this assembly verse.
Cites Deuteronomy 31:12, the verse about assembling the people, as the text under discussion.
Reports Rabbi Elazar ben Azarya's reading: women come to listen, and children come so their bringers are rewarded.
Rabbi Yehoshua praises this teaching as a pearl the students had tried to keep from him.
Rabbi Elazar's further homily on Deuteronomy 26:17-18, where God and Israel affirm one another.
God tells Israel that as they made Him one unique entity, He will make them one unique nation.
Repeats the point that Israel has made God unique in the world.
Cites the Shema, 'the Lord our God, the Lord is One' (Deuteronomy 6:4), as the basis for that point.
Concludes that God will make Israel one unique nation in the world, as stated; the passage breaks off.

ranges.en: Opens by citing I Chronicles 17:21 on Israel as one nation in the land, as a source for the unity theme.
Notes that Rabbi Elazar ben Azarya also opened his lecture with expositions.
Quotes Ecclesiastes 12:11 comparing the words of the wise to goads and nails given by one shepherd.
Explains the goad analogy: Torah words direct learners from the path of death to the path of life.
Asks: if the goad is movable, Torah should also be changeable, so why does the verse compare it to nails?
Pursues the same analogy: nails diminish, so Torah diminishes; the verse's 'well fastened' is then questioned.
Explains that Torah flourishes like a planted shoot, and that scholars in groups debate and reach differing rulings.
Asks how a person can learn Torah when its opinions conflict so widely.
Answers with the verse that all were given by one shepherd, so the many opinions share one source.
Explains that one God gave the Torah and one leader, Moses, transmitted it from the Master of all creation.
Cites Exodus 20:1, 'And God spoke all these words', with the plural 'words' meaning all interpretations were given.
Advises the student to make his ears like a funnel and hear all opinions, pure and impure, prohibiting and permitting.
Rabbi Yehoshua declares that no generation is orphaned while Rabbi Elazar ben Azarya dwells in it.
Asks why the two sages did not directly tell Rabbi Yehoshua Rabbi Elazar's teachings without delay.
Answers that they hesitated because of an earlier incident.
Relates a baraita about Rabbi Yosei ben Durmaskit, who was asked for a novel idea when greeting Rabbi Elazar in Lod.
Yosei reports the Sages' vote that the poor man's tithe is separated in Ammon and Moab during the Sabbatical Year.
Rabbi Elazar rebukes Yosei harshly, telling him to catch his eyes that are about to pop out.
Rabbi Elazar weeps and cites Psalms 25:14 on God's counsel with those who fear Him, as the Sages reached the right ruling.
Rabbi Elazar tells Yosei the Sages need not worry: the halakha is a tradition from Sinai transmitted through Rabban Yoḥanan ben Zakkai.
Asks what the reason is for the difference between those who returned from Egypt and those from Babylonia.
Explains that the Egyptian conquest sanctified the land only for its time, so Babylonian returnees left those cities for the poor's tithe.
Reports that Rabbi Elazar's mind was eased, he prayed for Yosei's eyes to return, and they did.
Cites a baraita defining an imbecile: one who goes out alone at night, sleeps in a cemetery, or tears his garment.
Rav Huna rules that one is an imbecile only when all these signs appear together.
Rabbi Yoḥanan rules that a single one of these signs suffices to classify one as an imbecile.
Asks what the circumstances are, since if the acts are deranged, one sign suffices, and if not, all of them do not.
Explains that the baraita concerns deranged acts, and that sleeping in a cemetery may be a deliberate attempt to attract an impure spirit.
Explains that going out alone at night may be self-cooling from fever and tearing clothes may be anxious distraction; performing all together still marks madness.

ranges.en: Offers an analogy: an ox that gores repeatedly becomes forewarned for every animal, as a model for repeated deranged acts.
Rav Pappa claims that Rav Huna would have retracted his view had he heard a certain baraita.
Cites the baraita defining an imbecile as one who destroys whatever is given to him, which Rav Pappa says would change Rav Huna's view.
Raises a dilemma: did Rav Huna retract only regarding tearing garments, or regarding all signs? It is left unresolved.
Cites the mishna listing the tumtum and hermaphrodite among those exempt from appearance.
Cites a baraita deriving from the verse's wording that women, tumtum, hermaphrodites are excluded and minors included.
The Master restates the baraita: 'males' excludes women.
Asks why a verse is needed to exclude women, since time-bound positive mitzvot are already exempt for women.
Answers that the verse is needed to block a verbal analogy with assembly, where women are obligated.
Restates the baraita: 'your males' excludes the tumtum and hermaphrodite.
Asks why the hermaphrodite must be excluded by verse, since he has a male aspect, and the baraita makes him a category of his own.
Asks whether a verse is needed to exclude the tumtum, whose status is a halakhic uncertainty.
Abaye answers that the verse concerns a tumtum whose testicles are visible externally, yet is still exempt.
The Master restates the baraita: 'all your males' includes minors.
Objects that the mishna exempts minors, which seems to contradict the baraita.
Abaye resolves it: the baraita refers to a minor who reached training age; the verse only supports a rabbinic obligation.
Asks what purpose 'all your males' serves if it is not needed for minors.
Cites the view of the Aherim, that scrimpers, copper melders and tanners are exempt, derived from 'all your males'.
Cites the mishna's exemption of women and unemancipated slaves.
Asks the source for the exemption of slaves, since women's exemption was derived earlier.
Rav Huna derives it from 'before the Lord God', meaning only one with a single master is obligated.
Asks why a verse is needed, since slaves follow women in every mitzva, through a verbal analogy with 'to her'.
Ravina answers the verse is needed only for one who is half slave and half free.
Argues from the mishna's precise wording, 'slaves who are not emancipated', that it refers to partly emancipated slaves.
Cites the mishna listing the lame, blind, sick and old as exempt from appearance.
Cites a baraita on 'regalim': excludes people with artificial legs and the lame, sick, blind, old, and one unable to walk.
Asks what the final category, one unable to ascend on his own feet, adds beyond the earlier exemptions.
Rava begins to answer that it comes to add a further case; the passage breaks off at the end of the daf.

ranges.en: Cites Isaiah 1:12 on trampling God's courts, read as the basis for exempting one who cannot enter barefoot.
Teaching: the uncircumcised and the ritually impure are exempt from the mitzva of appearance.
Derives the impure person's exemption from the paired verses 'and there you shall come' and 'and there you shall bring'.
Asks from where the uncircumcised person's exemption is derived.
Identifies the source as Rabbi Akiva, who includes the uncircumcised with the impure via the doubled 'ish ish' in Leviticus 22:4.
Cites a baraita with the same verses, teaching that the impure person is exempt because he may not enter.
Cites the baraita of Yoḥanan ben Dehavai in Rabbi Yehuda's name: one blind in one eye is exempt, from the verse's wordplay on seeing.
Rav Huna weeps at the verse and says a servant whose master expects to see him would be distanced, citing Isaiah 1:12.
Rav Huna again weeps at a verse on sacrifice and eating at the master's table, citing Isaiah 1:11.
Rabbi Elazar weeps at Joseph's brothers being unable to answer him, and reasons that God's rebuke is all the more severe.
Rabbi Elazar weeps again at the next verse, introducing the Samuel passage.
Cites I Samuel 28:15, Samuel's words to Saul: 'Why have you disquieted me, to bring me up?'
Reasons that if the righteous Samuel feared judgment, then all the more so should we fear it.
Asks what Samuel feared, given the verse describing the apparition.
Cites I Samuel 28:13, 'I see godlike beings coming up', and infers from the plural 'olim' that two figures appeared.
Answers that the second figure was Moses, whom Samuel brought to testify that he fulfilled the Torah.
Rabbi Ami weeps at the verse on the sinner's mouth in the dust, introducing his reaction.
Cites Lamentations 3:29, 'let him put his mouth in the dust, perhaps there may be hope'.
Rabbi Ami objects that a sinner suffers so much that hope is only a perhaps.
Rabbi Ami weeps at the next verse, introducing the Zephaniah passage.
Cites Zephaniah 2:3, 'seek righteousness, seek humility, perhaps you shall be hidden on the day of God's anger'.
Rabbi Ami objects that all this is required of each person, yet hiding is only a perhaps.
Rabbi Asi weeps at the verse on hating evil and loving good, introducing the Amos passage.
Cites Amos 5:15 on hating evil and establishing justice in the gate, with 'perhaps God will be gracious'.
Rabbi Asi objects that such great demands are met with only a perhaps.
Rav Yosef weeps at the next verse, introducing the Proverbs passage.
Cites Proverbs 13:23, 'there are those swept away without justice'.
Asks whether anyone dies before his time without reason.
Answers yes, citing the case of Rav Beivai bar Abaye, who saw people die at the Angel of Death's hands.
Narrates how the Angel of Death sent an agent to fetch Miriam the hair-braider, a case of a mistaken death.
The agent instead brings Miriam the child-raiser, the wrong woman.
The Angel of Death says to return her, but since she was brought she is counted among the dead.
Rav Beivai asks how the agent could kill her before her appointed time.
The agent replies that she was holding a shovel and was lighting a fire with it, so the opportunity arose.

ranges.en: Narrates the continuation of the earlier case: the woman scalded her foot and her luck failed, enabling the Angel of Death to take her.
Rav Beivai bar Abaye asks the Angel of Death by what right he takes someone before his time.
The Angel of Death replies by citing Proverbs 13:23, 'there are those swept away without justice'.
Rav Beivai counters with Ecclesiastes 1:4, 'one generation passes and another comes', implying a fixed lifespan per generation.
The Angel of Death explains he shepherds each generation until its years are complete, then hands them to the angel Duma.
Rav Beivai asks what the Angel of Death does with the extra years of those taken early.
Answers that extra years are added to a Torah scholar who overlooks personal insults, so he replaces the deceased for that time.
Rabbi Yoḥanan weeps at the verse on the Satan's incitement against Job.
Cites Job 2:3, God telling the Satan that he incited Him against Job to destroy him without cause.
Rabbi Yoḥanan asks whether a slave whose master is incited against him has any remedy.
Rabbi Yoḥanan weeps again at the next verse from Job.
Cites Job 15:15, 'Behold, He puts no trust in His sacred ones', to support the claim that God takes some early.
Anecdote: Rabbi Yoḥanan sees a man picking unripe figs and keeping them, a picture of God taking the righteous early.
Rabbi Yoḥanan explains the anecdote: God takes some righteous people early because He knows they will stumble later.
Asks whether this is so, since a student of Rabbi Alexandri died young.
Rabbi Alexandri concluded the student's early death was due to his own actions, and suggests he may have been one of the untrusted ones.
Answers that this student had been disrespectful toward his teachers, which Rabbi Alexandri knew about.
Rabbi Yoḥanan weeps at the verse in Malachi 3:5 about the swift witness against sinners.
Cites Malachi 3:5 in full: God will be a swift witness against sorcerers, adulterers and those who oppress the hireling.
Asks whether a slave whose master judges him swiftly has any remedy.
Rabbi Yoḥanan ben Zakkai laments that the verse weighs lenient mitzvot the same as severe ones.
Reish Lakish rules that one who distorts a convert's judgment is as if he distorted God's judgment.
Grounds Reish Lakish's ruling in the wordplay 'umattei' in Malachi 3:5, read as 'turn Me aside'.
Rabbi Ḥanina bar Pappa rules that one who regrets a sin is forgiven immediately.
Grounds that ruling in Malachi 3:5, 'and do not fear Me', which implies that fearing God brings immediate forgiveness.
Rabbi Yoḥanan weeps at the verse on God bringing every work into judgment.
Cites Ecclesiastes 12:14 on God judging every hidden thing.
Rabbi Yoḥanan asks whether a slave whose master weighs unwitting sins like intentional ones has a remedy.
Asks what hidden sin the verse refers to.
Rav says it refers to one who kills a louse in front of another, disgusting him.
Shmuel says it refers to one who spits in front of another, disgusting him.
Asks what the phrase 'whether good or evil' in Ecclesiastes 12:14 means.
Yannai's school: it refers to one who gives charity to a poor man publicly, embarrassing him.
Anecdote: Rabbi Yannai rebukes a man who gave a dinar publicly, saying it would have been better not to give it at all.
Rabbi Sheila's school: it refers to one who gives charity to a woman privately, drawing suspicion of improper conduct.
Rava: it refers to one who sends his wife unsliced meat on Shabbat eve, risking that she cooks forbidden sciatic nerve.
Asks: but Rava himself sent such meat to his wife on Shabbat eve.
Answers that Rav Ḥisda's daughter was a known expert whom Rava trusted to notice the forbidden fat.
Rabbi Yoḥanan weeps at Deuteronomy 31:21 on the many evils and troubles that come upon the people.
Cites Deuteronomy 31:21, 'Then it shall come to pass, when many evils and troubles are come upon them'.
Rabbi Yoḥanan asks whether a slave whose master brings evils and troubles upon him has any remedy.
Asks what 'evils and troubles' means in the verse.
Rav: evils that cause troubles for one another, like the remedies for a hornet sting and a scorpion sting conflicting.
Shmuel: it refers to one who lends money to a poor man in distress, then presses him for repayment immediately.
Rava explains a folk saying: money to an insolvent person is hard to find, but creditors make it appear when pressed.
Cites Deuteronomy 31:17 on God hiding His face and the people being devoured.
Rav rules that anyone not subject to God's hiding of the face is not of the Jewish people; the passage breaks off at the end of the daf.

Rakia is where the sun, moon, stars and zodiac signs are fixed.
Genesis 1:17 says God set them in the firmament of the heaven.
Sheḥakim is where mills grind manna for the righteous.
Psalms 78:23-24 describes the heights above, the doors of heaven, and manna rained down for food.
Zevul is the heavenly Jerusalem and Temple, where the angel Michael offers a sacrifice on the heavenly altar.
I Kings 8:13 speaks of a house of Zevul built for God as an everlasting dwelling.
Asks how we know that Zevul is called heaven.
Isaiah 63:15: look down from heaven and see, from Your holy and glorious abode.
Ma'on is where angels sing at night and fall silent by day out of respect for Israel.
Psalms 42:9: by day the Lord commands His kindness, and at night His song is with me.
Reish Lakish: whoever studies Torah at night has a thread of kindness drawn over him by day.
Psalms 42:9 is cited for the claim that God commands kindness by day.
Asks what the reason is that God commands kindness by day.
Because the night is His song, meaning the song of Torah.
Another version of Reish Lakish: Torah study in this world, like night, earns kindness in the World-to-Come, like day.
Psalms 42:9 supports the parallel between night and this world, and day and the World-to-Come.
Rabbi Levi: one who interrupts Torah for idle talk is fed the coals of the broom tree.
Job 30:4, about plucking saltwort and broom roots, is read as an allusion to the tablets of Torah and idle talk.
Asks how we know that Ma'on is called heaven.
Deuteronomy 26:15: look forth from Your holy Ma'on, from heaven, the dwelling place of Your abode.
Makhon holds storehouses of snow, hail, harmful dew, storms and mist, with fire doors, implying storehouses of evil.
Deuteronomy 28:12 speaks of God's good storehouse, the heavens, implying a storehouse of the opposite.
Asks whether these things are in heaven, since they are clearly on earth.
Psalms 148:7-8: praise the Lord from the earth, sea monsters, fire, hail, snow and stormy wind.
Rav Yehuda cites Rav: David asked God to bring these forces down from heaven to earth.
David's plea quotes Psalms 5:5: You are not a God who desires wickedness, and evil shall not sojourn with You.
Asks how we know that this place is called heaven.
I Kings 8:39: and You shall hear in heaven, the dwelling place of Your abode.
Aravot is the firmament holding righteousness, justice, charity, treasuries of life, peace and blessing, and the souls of the righteous.
Verses from Psalms, Isaiah, Judges, Psalms and Samuel support that these treasuries and souls are found in heaven.
Spirits and souls yet to be created are found in heaven.
Isaiah 57:16 says the spirit and the souls come from God.
The dew with which God will revive the dead is found in heaven.
Psalms 68:10 speaks of a bountiful rain that God pours down on His inheritance.
In the firmaments dwell the ofanim, seraphim, holy creatures, ministering angels and the Throne of Glory, with God above in Aravot.
Psalms 68:5: extol Him who rides upon the skies, Aravot, whose name is God.
Asks how we know that Aravot is called heaven.
A verbal analogy: rides appears in Psalms 68:5 about Aravot and in Deuteronomy 33:26 about heaven.
Darkness, clouds and fog surround God.
Psalms 18:12 says God made darkness His hiding place and thick clouds His pavilion.
Asks whether there is darkness before God, since light is said to dwell with Him.
Objects from Daniel 2:22 that God knows what is in the darkness and that light dwells with Him.
Replies that there is no real difficulty, and the two verses are reconciled.

13a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Explains that the darkness verse refers to the outer houses, while the inner houses contain only light.
Rav Aha bar Yaakov says there is one more firmament above the heads of the divine creatures.
Ezekiel 1:22 describes a firmament above the creatures' heads, with the color of terrible ice.
Sets a limit on speech: one may speak up to this point and no further.
Ben Sira's teaching: do not seek what is beyond you or probe what is hidden; attend to what is permitted.
A baraita introduces Rabban Yohanan ben Zakkai's account of a Divine Voice answering a wicked king.
Asks what response the Divine Voice gave to that wicked man.
The Divine Voice rebukes the wicked king as a descendant of Nimrod, who incited the whole world against God, quoting Isaiah 14:14.
Asks how many years a man lives.
Seventy years.
Psalms 90:10: seventy years, or eighty if one is strong.
Gives distances: a 500-year walk from earth to the firmament, the same for the firmament's thickness and between firmaments.
The holy creatures stand above the firmaments, their limbs corresponding to all of them, with the Throne of Glory above them.
Rebukes Nebuchadnezzar: he said he would ascend above the clouds and be like the Most High.
Isaiah 14:15: yet you shall be brought down to the netherworld, to the uttermost parts of the pit.
The mishna forbids expounding the Chariot to an individual.
Rabbi Hiyya taught that one may transmit its outlines to an individual, leaving him to understand the rest.
Rabbi Zeira: outlines may be transmitted only to the court president and to one whose heart is troubled over sin.
Rabbi Ami: the secrets of Torah are transmitted only to one who has five qualities.
Isaiah 3:3 lists the five qualities: captain of fifty, man of favor, counselor, cunning charmer, skilled enchanter.
Rabbi Ami: Torah teachings may not be transmitted to a gentile.
Psalms 147:20: He has not dealt so with any nation, and they have not known His ordinances.
Rabbi Yohanan offers to teach Rabbi Elazar the Design of the Divine Chariot.
Rabbi Elazar replies that he has not yet aged enough, and by then Rabbi Yohanan had died.
Rabbi Asi offers to teach Rabbi Elazar the Design of the Chariot.
Rabbi Elazar replies that had he merited it, he would have learned it from Rabbi Yohanan, his teacher.
Rav Yosef, your teacher, knew the Chariot, while the elders of Pumbedita studied the Creation.
The elders of Pumbedita ask Rav Yosef to teach them the Chariot.
He asks them first to teach him the Creation, and they do.
They ask again to be taught the Design of the Chariot.
Rav Yosef replies that such secrets were taught in a tradition and must remain private.
Song of Songs 4:11: honey and milk under your tongue, meaning sweet matters should stay unspoken.
Rabbi Abbahu says the same principle is derived from here.
Proverbs 27:26, read as kevashim: concealed matters belong under your clothing and must not be revealed.
The elders say they have learned the Ezekiel passages up to a certain point.
Ezekiel 2:1: and He said to me, son of man, which is where they stopped.
Rav Yosef responds that these verses are the very essence of the Chariot, containing its main details.
A baraita objects that the Chariot is taught only up to a certain verse, contrary to Rav Yosef.
Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi says to 'and I saw', and Rabbi Yitzhak says to 'the electrum', in Ezekiel 1:27.
Reconciles: the worthy are taught up to 'and I saw', then only outlines, and a wise student may be taught on his own.
Asks whether one may teach about the electrum at all.
Objects that a youth who expounded the electrum was consumed by fire.
Replies that the youth was different, since his time for such study had not yet come.
Rav Yehuda: Hananya ben Hizkiya is remembered for good, since Ezekiel's words seemed to contradict the Torah and it nearly was suppressed.
Asks what Hananya ben Hizkiya did.
They brought him three hundred barrels of oil, and he sat in an upper chamber and expounded Ezekiel to reconcile it with Torah.
A baraita: a youth reading Ezekiel was burned by fire from the electrum, and Hananya argued that not everyone can understand it.
Asks what the electrum is.

13b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: A baraita: the fiery living creatures sometimes fall silent and sometimes speak, depending on whether God's voice issues forth.
Ezekiel 1:14 describes the creatures running and returning like the appearance of a lightning flash.
Asks what running and returning means.
Rav Yehuda: like fire emitted from a furnace, its flame bursting out and withdrawing.
Asks what the image of the lightning flash means.
Rabbi Yosei bar Hanina: like fire emitted from between pieces of earthenware used in refining gold.
Ezekiel 1:4 describes a stormy wind, a great cloud, and fire from whose midst came something like electrum.
Asks where that wind went.
It went to subdue the world under Nebuchadnezzar so nations would not mock Israel, and God says Israel's sins made Him serve idol worshippers.
Ezekiel 1:15 describes a wheel upon the earth near the creatures.
Rabbi Elazar: that wheel is an angel standing on the earth whose head reaches the creatures.
A baraita names this angel Sandalfon, who stands behind the Chariot and weaves crowns for his Maker.
Objects that crowns cannot be woven for God, since Ezekiel 3:12 says His place is unknown to anyone.
Rather, one says a name for the crown, and it sits on God's head of its own accord.
Rava: Isaiah saw all that Ezekiel saw but described less; Ezekiel is like a villager amazed by the palace, Isaiah like a city dweller focused on the king.
Reish Lakish asks the meaning of I will sing to the Lord for He is highly exalted in Exodus 15:1.
Sing to the One exalted above the exalted: the lion, ox, eagle and man each rule their kind, but God is above all.
The Master's teaching: lion, ox, eagle and man are the creatures of the Chariot, and God is exalted above them all.
Ezekiel 1:10 and Ezekiel 10:14 both list the faces of the creatures, with differing lists.
Objects that the ox's face is missing from the list in Ezekiel 10:14.
Reish Lakish: Ezekiel asked mercy for the ox face, which was turned into a cherub, since an accuser should not become a defender.
Asks what cherub means.
Rabbi Abbahu: like a baby, keravya, since in Babylonia a baby is called ravya.
Rav Pappa asks Abaye: if so, Ezekiel 1:10 lists cherub and man as separate faces, so what is the difference?
Abaye: the face of a man is a large face, while the face of a cherub is the small face of a baby.
Objects that Isaiah 6:2 gives each creature six wings, while Ezekiel 1:6 gives four, a contradiction.
Replies that the six-wing verse refers to when the Temple stands, and the four-wing verse to when it does not.
Rav Hananel: the wings that were diminished are those with which they sing song.
Isaiah 6:2-3 says they flew and called, and Proverbs 23:5 says the flight ceased, supporting the loss of wings.
The Rabbis: the wings that were lost are those with which the creatures cover their feet.
Ezekiel 1:7 says their feet were straight, implying their feet were uncovered.
Objects that this proof is inconclusive, since the feet may have been revealed briefly; otherwise the face verse would also imply lost wings.
Rather, the creatures were revealed momentarily, so the feet and faces were both seen.
Refutes this: a face may be revealed before the Master, but feet should not be, so their wings must have been lost.
Objects to contradictions: Daniel 7:10 counts thousands of thousands, while Job 25:3 asks whether His troops can be numbered.
Replies that the verses refer to two periods: when the Temple stands, and when it does not, when the heavenly entourage was diminished.
Baraita: Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi, in the name of Abba Yosei ben Dosai: thousands of thousands is one troop, while His troops are uncountable.
Rabbi Yirmeya bar Abba: Daniel 7:10 refers to the River Dinur, which the thousands of thousands serve.
Daniel 7:10: a fiery river issued forth, served by thousands of thousands.
Asks where the river issues from.
From the perspiration of the divine creatures.
Asks where the river flows to.
Rav: upon the heads of the wicked in Gehenna. Rav Aha bar Yaakov: over those snatched away before their time.
Jeremiah 23:19: the whirling storm of the Lord shall whirl upon the heads of the wicked.
Rav Aha bar Yaakov: the river flows over those who were snatched away.
Job 22:16: those snatched away before their time, whose foundation was poured out like a stream.
Baraita: Rabbi Shimon HaHasid says those snatched away are the 974 generations that were not created.

14a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Generations that were to be created before the world but were not; God planted some in each generation as its insolent ones.
Rav Nachman bar Yitzhak: the Job verse about those snatched away is a blessing for Torah scholars who humble themselves.
Job 22:16, whose foundation was poured out as a stream, implies that God gives them an abundance of secret knowledge.
Shmuel: each day angels are created from the River Dinur, sing, and then cease to exist.
Lamentations 3:23: they are new every morning, great is Your faithfulness.
Rabbi Shmuel bar Naḥmani, citing Rabbi Yonatan: an angel is created from each word emerging from God's mouth.
Psalms 33:6: by the word of the Lord the heavens were made, and by the breath of His mouth all their hosts.
Two verses seem to conflict on God's appearance: Daniel 7:9 describes white hair, while Song of Songs 5:11 describes black locks.
Not difficult: in the academy the old man's image applies, and at war the youthful image applies.
Daniel 7:9 mentions a fiery throne, and another phrase speaks of thrones placed, implying two thrones.
One throne is for God and one for David, according to Rabbi Akiva.
Rabbi Yosei HaGelili rebukes Akiva for profaning the Divine Presence by seating another beside God.
Rather, one throne is for judgment and the other for righteousness.
Asks whether Rabbi Akiva accepted this rebuke or not.
A baraita teaching Akiva's view that one throne is for judgment and one for righteousness is brought as evidence.
Rabbi Elazar ben Azarya rebukes Akiva for occupying himself with aggada rather than the halakhot of leprosy and impurity.
Rather, the two thrones are a seat for sitting and a small seat as a footstool.
Isaiah 66:1: the heavens are My seat and the earth My footstool.
Rav Dimi: Isaiah cursed Israel with eighteen curses and was not calmed until he added the great curse of Isaiah 3:5.
Isaiah 3:5: the child shall behave insolently against the aged, and the base against the honorable.
Asks what the eighteen curses are.
Cites Isaiah 3:1-4, listing the items to be removed from Israel, from support and staff to children and babes ruling.
Explains support as Bible masters and staff as Mishna masters, with a disagreement over how many orders they knew.
Explains bread as Talmud masters, water as aggada masters, and the mighty man, war man, judge, prophet, diviner and elder as various roles.
Captain of fifty means one who can engage with the five books of the Torah, and no one under fifty should be appointed to teach the public.
The man of favor is one who wins favor for his generation: Rabbi Hanina ben Dosa above, and Rabbi Abbahu below before the emperor.
Counselor is a calendar expert; cunning is a student who makes his rabbis wise by his questions.
The charmer is so profound that listeners become as though deaf to his words.
The skillful one derives something new from one text to another, and the enchanter is fit to receive secrets transmitted in whispers.
Asks the meaning of I will make children their princes.
Rabbi Elazar: children means people devoid of mitzvot, who will become leaders of the nation.
Rav Pappa bar Yaakov: babes means foxes, sons of foxes, inferior in deeds and in lineage.
Isaiah 3:5 quoted: the child behaves insolently toward the aged, and the base toward the honorable.
The child lacks mitzvot and insults the one full of them; the base treats major sins as minor, insulting one who treats even minor ones as major.
Rav Ketina: even at Jerusalem's downfall, trustworthy men did not cease among its people.
Isaiah 3:6: a man will take hold of his brother and say, you have a cloak, be our ruler.
Asks the meaning of and this stumbling block in Isaiah 3:6.
The stumbling block refers to matters people grasp only after stumbling, which are under the addressed man's hand.
Explains yissa in Isaiah 3:7 as an oath, so the man swears he will not be a healer, meaning a sitter in the study hall.
Exodus 20:6: you shall not take the name of the Lord your God in vain, showing yissa means swearing.
He swears he was never among those who sit in the study hall, having no knowledge of Bible, Mishna or Gemara.
Objects that perhaps the case differs: a man claiming learning would be asked to recite, so his denial proves nothing.
Replies that a liar would have claimed he learned and forgot; I will not be a healer means he never learned.
Objects with Rava's teaching that Jerusalem was not destroyed until trustworthy men ceased, citing Jeremiah 5:1.
Replies that the difficulty is not real.

14b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: One case concerns Torah matters, where the sages were trustworthy, and the other concerns commerce, where they were not.
Narrative: Rabban Yohanan ben Zakkai rides a donkey while his student Rabbi Elazar ben Arakh asks him to teach a chapter on the Chariot.
Yohanan refuses, citing the mishna that the Chariot is not taught to one person unless he is wise and understands on his own.
Elazar asks permission to first recite one point he learned from his teacher.
Yohanan tells him to speak.
Yohanan dismounts, covers his head in reverence, and sits on a stone under an olive tree.
Elazar asks why his teacher dismounted.
Yohanan explains that while the Chariot is expounded with the Divine Presence and angels present, he cannot ride a donkey.
Elazar expounds, fire descends and encircles the trees of the field, and the trees break into song.
Asks what song the trees sang.
Psalms 148:7-14: praise the Lord from the earth, sea monsters, fruit trees and cedars.
An angel answers from the fire that this is the very Design of the Chariot, as Elazar expounded it.
Yohanan kisses Elazar's head and blesses God for a son like him, who understands, investigates and expounds the Chariot.
Yohanan praises Elazar as rare: he both expounds the verses well and fulfills the commandments, a credit to Abraham.
When this was recounted to Rabbi Yehoshua, he and Rabbi Yosei the Priest decide to expound the Chariot too, and that day a rainbow-like cloud appears.
Angels gather to listen, like people gathering to watch the rejoicing of a bride and groom.
Rabbi Yosei the Priest reports this to Yohanan, who blesses them and recounts a dream about an invitation to the third group.
Objects: is that so? A baraita lists the lecturers on the Chariot, which seems to contradict the claim.
The baraita of Rabbi Yosei son of Rabbi Yehuda: three lectures, given by Yehoshua, Akiva and Hananya ben Hakhinai.
Objects that Elazar ben Arakh, who lectured before Yohanan, is not counted in this list.
Resolves: only those who both lectured and were lectured to are counted, not those who lectured without being taught.
Objects that Hananya ben Hakhinai, who was not lectured to, is counted anyway.
Replies that Hananya lectured before one who had lectured to his own rabbi, so he qualifies.
Baraita: four entered the pardes, namely ben Azzai, ben Zoma, Aher and Rabbi Akiva.
Akiva warns them: at the pure marble stones, do not say water, water.
Psalms 101:7: he who speaks falsehood shall not be established before My eyes.
Ben Azzai glimpsed at the Divine Presence and died.
Psalms 116:15: precious in the eyes of the Lord is the death of His pious ones.
Ben Zoma glimpsed and was harmed.
Proverbs 25:16: eat only what suffices, lest you become full and vomit it, applied to ben Zoma.
Aher cut down the saplings, becoming a heretic, while Rabbi Akiva exited in peace.
Asks ben Zoma the halakha on castrating a dog.
Ben Zoma derives from Leviticus 22:24 that such castration is forbidden for any animal in your land.
Asks whether a High Priest may marry a woman presumed a virgin who became pregnant, depending on Shmuel's view.

15a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Asks whether a man can have intercourse without drawing blood, or whether Shmuel's case is too rare to matter.
Shmuel's case is rare, so we fear she conceived after washing in a bath containing semen.
Objects: did not Shmuel say semen not shot like an arrow cannot fertilize, which would make conception impossible?
Replies that the semen was initially shot like an arrow and could fertilize at a later moment.
Narrative: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Hananya stood on a step on the Temple Mount, and ben Zoma passed without honoring him, lost in thought.
Yehoshua asks where ben Zoma is coming from and going to, meaning what is on his mind.
Ben Zoma reports he contemplated Creation: the gap between the upper and lower waters is three fingers, like a dove hovering without touching.
Yehoshua tells his students that ben Zoma is still outside and has not yet fully grasped these matters.
Objects that the hovering verse refers to day one, while the separation of the waters was on day two, undermining ben Zoma's proof.
Gives the measure of the gap: a thread's thickness, the space between bridge boards, two spread robes, or two cups placed one on another.
Aher cut down the saplings, becoming a heretic.
Ecclesiastes 5:5: do not let your mouth bring your flesh into guilt.
Asks what led Aher to heresy.
He saw Metatron seated and writing the merits of Israel, and reasoned that nothing sits above, so there must be two powers.
They removed Metatron from heaven and struck him with sixty fiery rods, so others would not err as Aher did.
Asks Metatron why he did not stand before Elisha ben Avuya.
Because he did not stand, Metatron was given permission to erase Aher's merits and cause him to stumble.
A Divine Voice calls Jeremiah 3:22, Return rebellious children, apart from Aher.
Elisha reasons that since he is banished from the World-to-Come, he will enjoy this world, and Aher went astray.
Aher finds a prostitute and solicits her.
She asks: are you not Elisha ben Avuya? Shall a man of your stature do such a thing?
He uprooted a radish on Shabbat and gave it to her, and she says he is now other, Aher.
After going astray, Aher asks Rabbi Meir a question.
Asks the meaning of God made the one as well as the other, Ecclesiastes 7:14.
Meir: whatever God created has a corresponding creation, such as mountains and hills, seas and rivers.
Aher says Akiva taught that everything has its opposite: righteous and wicked, Eden and Gehenna, each person with two portions.
Rav Mesharshiyya derives double portions from Isaiah 61:7 for the righteous and Jeremiah 17:18 for the wicked.
Aher asks Meir about Job 28:17: gold and glass cannot equal it, and its exchange is not vessels of fine gold.
Meir: words of Torah are as hard to acquire as gold but as easy to lose as glass.
Aher says Akiva taught that a Torah scholar who has sinned has a remedy, as broken gold and glass can be remelted.
Meir tells Aher that he too should return.
Aher replies that he has heard behind the curtain the voice saying Return, rebellious children, apart from Aher.
Baraita: Aher rode a horse on Shabbat while Rabbi Meir walked behind him to learn Torah from him.
Aher tells Meir to turn back, having measured the Shabbat boundary by his horse's steps.
Meir tells him to return to the right path as well.
Aher again cites the voice behind the curtain: Return, rebellious children, apart from Aher.
Meir takes hold of Aher and brings him into the study hall.
Aher asks a child to recite his verse to him, as a form of divination.
Isaiah 48:22: there is no peace, says the Lord, for the wicked.
Aher brings him to another study hall.
Aher again asks a child to recite his verse to him.
Jeremiah 2:22: though you wash with niter and use much soap, your iniquity is marked before Me.
Aher brings him to yet another study hall.

15b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Aher again asks a child to recite his verse to him.
Jeremiah 4:30: the spoiled one who adorns herself in vain, a picture of the hopelessness of the wicked.
Aher brings the child to another study hall, and then to thirteen synagogues, where every child recites similar verses about the wicked.
Aher asks the last child to recite his verse.
Psalms 50:16: but to the wicked God says, what right have you to recite My statutes.
The child stuttered, so it sounded like to Elisha God says, which Elisha took as a deliberate insult.
Some say Aher had a knife, tore the child apart, and sent him to the thirteen synagogues.
Others say Aher merely said he would have torn the child apart had he had a knife.
The Heavenly Court rules Aher is not judged by his deeds because of his Torah study, nor admitted to the World-to-Come because of his sin.
Rabbi Meir wishes Aher judged properly and admitted, and says he will cause smoke to rise from his grave; when Meir died, smoke rose.
Rabbi Yoḥanan questions Meir's act, then arranges for the smoke to be extinguished when he dies; a eulogizer praises him.
Aher's daughter comes to Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi seeking sustenance and says she is Aher's daughter.
Yehuda HaNasi asks whether any of Aher's seed remains in the world.
Job 18:19: he shall have neither son nor grandson among his people, nor any remaining in his dwellings.
She replies: remember his Torah, and do not remember his deeds.
Fire licked Yehuda's bench; he wept, reasoning that if God honors those who despised Torah, how much more those who honor it.
Asks how Rabbi Meir could learn Torah from Aher's mouth.
Objects: Rabbi Yoḥanan taught that Torah is sought only from a teacher who is like an angel of the Lord, which Aher was not.
Malachi 2:7: if the teacher is like an angel of the Lord, seek Torah from his mouth; otherwise, do not.
Reish Lakish: Meir read Proverbs 22:17 as to My knowledge rather than their knowledge, so one heeds Sages whose view matches God's.
Rav Ḥanina: Psalms 45:11, listen daughter and forget your people, supports heeding a Sage's teaching while ignoring his faults.
Objects that the two sources contradict: learn only from a perfect teacher, versus learn even from one of flawed character.
Replies: the permissive case refers to an adult, the restrictive case to a minor who must learn from a righteous teacher.
Rav Dimi reports that in the West they say Rabbi Meir ate the fruit of a date and threw the peel away.
Rava cites Song of Songs 6:11: I went down into the garden of nuts to look at the green plants of the valley.
Asks why Torah scholars are compared to nuts.
Like a nut soiled outside whose contents stay pure, a scholar who has sinned keeps his Torah undefiled.
Rabba bar Sheila finds Elijah the prophet.
Rabba asks Elijah what the Holy One is doing.
Elijah: God is stating the halakhot of all the Sages, but not in Meir's name.
Asks why.
Because Meir learned halakhot from Aher's mouth.
Asks why Meir should be judged for that.
Elijah: Meir ate a pomegranate's contents and discarded the peel, so his defense has been heard above.
God laments: when a person suffers, the Divine Presence cries woe is Me from My head; if God grieves the blood of the wicked, how much more the righteous.
Shmuel found Rav Yehuda leaning on a doorpost, weeping.
Shmuel asks what he is crying about.
Isaiah 33:18: the Sages counted every letter, weighed minor and major transgressions, and taught 300 halakhot on a floating closet.
Rabbi Ami: Doeg asked Ahithophel 300 questions about the floating closet, both great scholars.
Mishna: three kings and four commoners have no portion in the World-to-Come, including Doeg and Ahithophel.
Asks: if such great scholars forfeited their portion, what will become of us?
Shinana replies that there was mud in their hearts; their flaws meant their Torah did not protect them.
Asks what Aher's failing was.
Greek tunes never left his mouth, and heretical books fell from his lap in the study hall, showing he was unsound from the start.
Nimos HaGardi, a gentile philosopher, asks Meir whether all wool entering the dye vat emerges colored.
Meir: whoever was clean from the start emerges worthy, and whoever was not clean from his mother's side does not.
Akiva ascended the orchard and descended safely.
Song of Songs 1:4: draw me, we will run after you; the king has brought me into his chambers.
Ministering angels sought to push Akiva out, but God told them to leave the elder, fit to serve His glory.

16a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Asks which verse Rabbi Akiva expounded to avoid Aher's error.
Rabba bar bar Hana reports Rabbi Yohanan's reading of the verse as marking God as unique among the myriads.
Deuteronomy 33:2 is cited, with 'ot' read as a sign of God's uniqueness among His myriads.
Rabbi Abbahu gives a parallel explanation of the same idea.
Song of Songs 5:10 is cited to show God is preeminent among His myriad.
Reish Lakish offers another explanation.
Isaiah 48:2 is cited to show God is the master of His host.
Rav Hiyya bar Abba reports Rabbi Yohanan's teaching on the verse.
I Kings 19:11-12 is cited: God was not in the wind, earthquake or fire, and Rabbi Akiva learned from it to avoid His place.
Introduces a baraita on the six traits shared by demons with angels and with humans.
Baraita: demons resemble ministering angels in having wings, flying across the world and knowing the future.
Objects that demons could not know the future, since not even angels do.
Upholds the baraita by saying demons only overhear what is revealed behind the curtain, as angels do.
Baraita: demons resemble humans in eating and drinking, multiplying and dying.
Baraita lists six traits of humans: three like angels, such as intelligence and upright posture, and three like animals.
Quotes the mishna: whoever contemplates four things would have been better off never coming into the world.
Asks why contemplating what preceded creation is forbidden, since that past cannot be changed.
Rabbi Yohanan and Rabbi Elazar explain with a parable of a king who forbids mention of his garbage dump.
Restates the mishna's point that one lacking concern for his Maker's honor should never have come into the world.
Asks what exactly counts as lacking concern for one's Maker's honor.
Rabbi Abba answers that it is looking at a rainbow.
Rav Yosef answers that it is committing a transgression in private, and states it in terms of looking at the rainbow.
Ezekiel 1:28 is cited to show that gazing at the rainbow is gazing at the likeness of God's glory.
Rav Yosef restates that the disrespect is committing a transgression in private.
Supports Rav Yosef's view with Rabbi Yitzhak's teaching that a private sinner pushes away the Divine Presence's feet.
Isaiah 66:1 is cited: heaven is God's throne and earth His footstool.
Objects that Rabbi Ela the Elder taught that a person should sin in private rather than desecrate God's name publicly.
Quotes Rabbi Ela the Elder's advice, which is the source for the objection.
Resolves the contradiction: one who can overcome his inclination should not sin, while one who cannot may sin privately.
Introduces Rabbi Yehuda bar Rabbi Nahmani, Reish Lakish's disseminator, expounding a teaching.
Teaches that one who gazes at three things grows dim-eyed: a rainbow, a prince and the priests.
Ezekiel 1:28 for the rainbow, and Numbers 27:20 for the prince, Moses, whose splendor rested upon him.
Explains the third case: looking at priests blessing Israel with the ineffable name while the Temple stood.
Reintroduces Rabbi Yehuda bar Rabbi Nahmani expounding another verse in Reish Lakish's name.
Asks what Micah 7:5 means.
Explains the verse: do not trust the evil inclination's promise that God will forgive.
Rea means the evil inclination (Genesis 8:21); Alluf means God (Jeremiah 3:4).
Raises the objection: who will testify against a person who sins in private?
Replies that the stones and beams of a person's house testify against him.
Habakkuk 2:11 is cited for the stones and beams testifying.
The Sages say that a person's soul testifies against him.
Micah 7:5 is cited: guard the doors of your mouth from her who lies in your bosom.
Asks what the 'one who lies in the bosom' in the verse refers to.
Answers that it is the soul.
Rabbi Zerika says the two ministering angels accompanying each person testify against him.
Psalms 91:11 is cited: God commands His angels to guard a person in all his ways.
The Sages say that a person's limbs testify against him.
Isaiah 43:12 is cited: you are My witnesses, so each person testifies against himself.
Mishna: Yosei ben Yoezer says not to lean on offerings on a festival.
Yosef ben Yohanan says one may lean on them.
Yehoshua ben Perachya says not to lean.

Yehuda ben Tabbai says not to lean.

Hillel and Menachem did not disagree on this matter.
Menachem left his post and Shammai took his place.
Shammai says not to lean.
Hillel says one may lean.

ranges.en: The first pairs of sages served as Nasi, with their counterparts as deputy heads of the court.
A baraita says three of the earlier pairs opposed placing hands and two of the later pairs permitted it, and served as Nasi.
Rabbi Meir's view on who served as Nasi and who as head of the court among these pairs.
The Sages' opposing view that Yehuda ben Tabbai was head of the court and Shimon ben Shataḥ the Nasi.
Asks which tanna taught the baraita about Yehuda ben Tabbai and the conspiring witness.
Identifies the baraita: Yehuda ben Tabbai swore he executed a conspiring witness to refute the Sadducees' view.
Shimon ben Shataḥ rebukes Yehuda for shedding innocent blood by executing the witness before both were found conspirators.
Cites the Sages' rule that conspiring witnesses are executed, flogged or fined only when both are found to be conspirators.
Yehuda ben Tabbai accepts never to issue a ruling except in the presence of Shimon ben Shataḥ.
Describes Yehuda ben Tabbai prostrating at the executed man's grave and people mistaking his weeping for the dead man's voice.
Yehuda tells the people it is his own voice, which will stop when he dies, and so it will be known.
Rav Aha son of Rava objects that the voice may have been appeased or prosecuted, so it proves nothing.
Asks whose opinion this baraita follows, first considering Rabbi Meir's view.
Explains that under Rabbi Meir's view Yehuda ruled in Shimon's presence because Shimon was the greater authority.
Asks why he needed the pledge under the Sages' view, since a deputy may rule in the presence of the Nasi.
Explains the pledge concerned joining others' rulings: he would not join before hearing Shimon ben Shataḥ.
Mishna: Menaḥem departed and Shammai entered his place.
Asks where Menaḥem went when he departed.
Abaye says Menaḥem went astray into evil ways.
Rava says Menaḥem left for service to the king.
A baraita confirms Rava: Menaḥem left for the king's service, taking eighty pairs of students in silk robes.
Rav Shemen bar Abba attributes to Rabbi Yoḥanan a warning not to treat a rabbinic decree lightly.
Rabbi Yoḥanan's point: placing hands on a Festival is a rabbinic prohibition, and great sages disputed it.
Asks why this needed saying, since a rabbinic decree tied to a mitzva is obviously serious.
Explains the statement excludes those who dispute the obligation itself, showing the dispute is over the rabbinic decree.
Rami bar Ḥama infers that placing hands requires pressing with all one's strength.
A baraita objects: Leviticus 1:2 implies sons place hands but daughters do not.
Rabbi Yosei and Rabbi Yishmael say it is optional for daughters of Israel to place hands.
Rabbi Yosei introduces an account he heard from Abba Elazar.
The account: a calf was brought to the Women's Courtyard and women placed hands on it purely to please them.
Infers from the account that placing hands with all one's strength is not required.
Replies that all one's strength is required, and the women were told to ease their hands.
Objects: if so, the women's act should be excluded because it is not placing hands at all, not because of pleasing them.
Rabbi Ami says the Gemara gave two reasons: it is not placing hands, and it was permitted to please the women.
Rav Pappa infers that the sides of an animal are prohibited just as those things forbidden to bear weight on Shabbat.

ranges.en: Rav Ashi concludes that a part near the back counts as the back, so the sides are not proven forbidden.
Mishna: Beit Shammai permit peace-offerings on a Festival without laying hands, and forbid burnt-offerings.
Beit Hillel permit both peace-offerings and burnt-offerings, with laying of hands on both.
Beit Shammai hold that when Shavuot falls on Shabbat eve, the slaughter day is the Sunday after Shabbat.
Beit Hillel reject postponing slaughter and concede it is after Shabbat only when Shavuot falls on Shabbat itself.
Mishna's practical result: the High Priest wears ordinary clothes and mourning and fasting are allowed, against the Sadducees.
Introduces Rabbi Elazar's teaching in the name of Rabbi Oshaya.
Asks from where we learn that Shavuot offerings can be made up for all seven days.
Deuteronomy 16:16 is cited, comparing Shavuot to Passover so that its offerings may be made up through seven days.
Objects that the verse may instead compare Shavuot to Sukkot, which has an eight-day makeup period.
Replies that the Eighth Day of Assembly is a separate Festival and not part of Sukkot.
Counters that the separate-Festival status may apply only to the six listed halakhot, not to makeup offerings.
Asserts that for makeup offerings the eighth day counts as makeup for the first day of the Festival.
Mishna: one who missed the first day of Sukkot may offer on the later days, supporting the makeup principle.
Principle: if you grasped many you grasped nothing, so comparing Shavuot to the smaller seven-day count is preferable.
Asks for what legal purpose the Torah wrote Sukkot in this comparison, if not to compare it to Shavuot.
Explains Sukkot is compared to Passover: as Passover requires overnight lodging in Jerusalem, so does Sukkot.
Asks from where we derive that Passover itself requires overnight lodging.

ranges.en: Deuteronomy 16:7 is cited: one turns in the morning and returns to his tents, so one may leave Jerusalem only in the morning.
Introduces the mishna case where Shavuot falls on the eve of Shabbat.
Beit Shammai say the slaughter day is after Shabbat.
Beit Hillel say Shavuot has no slaughter day at all.
Asks whether Beit Hillel mean there are no redress days at all for Shavuot.
Beit Hillel mean only that Shavuot does not need a slaughter day, since it is sacrificed on the Festival itself.
Asks what the mishna teaches by restating a dispute already given earlier, and notes that dispute was taught before.
Mishna: Beit Shammai permit peace-offerings but not burnt-offerings on a Festival; Beit Hillel permit both.
Explains both cases had to be taught, since each case alone would suggest the opposing school agrees on the other.
Baraita: one who missed the Festival offerings on the first day of Shavuot may not celebrate them later.
Asks whether the baraita's first-day-of-Shavuot wording implies there is one slaughter day, and so no redress days.
Baraita: the Torah counts days to Shavuot as it counts months, sanctifying Shavuot as a week of days.
Infers from the month analogy that Shavuot is only one day, with no redress days.
Rava objects that Shavuot counts days but not weeks, which contradicts this inference.
Abaye's teaching: counting days and counting weeks are both commanded for Shavuot, and Shavuot is established by weeks.
Teaching of the school of Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov: Leviticus 23:21-22 links Shavuot to a day of reaping, a weekday with festive character.
Analyzes the reaping verse: it must refer to redress days, since reaping is forbidden on the Festival day itself.
Explains why both teachings are needed: Rabbi Elazar's comparison alone would wrongly forbid work, so Ben Yaakov's ruling permits reaping.

ranges.en: Says the Gemara would not know how many redress days there are without a teaching on the matter.
Gives Rabbi Elazar's teaching in the name of Rabbi Oshaya that there are seven days of redress.
Introduces Reish Lakish's separate proof for the same point.
Exodus 23:16 calls Shavuot the festival of harvest, so reaping is done on the redress days of Shavuot.
Asks when that reaping happens, since reaping on the Festival day itself would be forbidden.
Rabbi Yohanan argues by analogy that the festival of gathering must refer to a season, so the same reading applies to Shavuot.
Infers that both Sages hold work on intermediate Festival days is forbidden by the Torah.
Asks what the biblical source is for prohibiting work on intermediate Festival days.
Exodus 23:15: the verse observe the Festival of Passover seven days teaches that work is prohibited on intermediate days.
Presents Rabbi Yoshiyya's view, and Rabbi Yonatan's view that the verse proof is unnecessary.
Rabbi Yonatan's a fortiori argument: if the first and seventh days are forbidden, intermediate days bounded by sanctity should be too.
Objects that the six days of Creation are bounded by sanctity yet permit work, so the argument fails.
Replies that weekdays lack an additional offering, unlike intermediate days, which have one.
Objects that the New Moon has an additional offering yet permits work.
Replies that the New Moon is not called a holy convocation, while intermediate days are, so work is forbidden on them.
A baraita on Leviticus 23:7 teaches that work is forbidden on intermediate days, per Rabbi Yosei the Galilean.
Attributes the baraita's ruling to Rabbi Yosei the Galilean, before Rabbi Akiva's dissent.
Rabbi Akiva says no verse is needed, since Leviticus 23:4 already speaks of appointed festivals.
Asks what subject the verse in that chapter addresses.
Argues the verse cannot refer to the first or seventh days, which already have a solemn rest, so it must refer to intermediate days.
A baraita on Deuteronomy 16:8 links the seventh day of Passover to the six intermediate days.
Objects that the link might make all six intermediate days fully forbidden, as the seventh day is.
Replies that the verse's pause indicates only the seventh day is fully forbidden, leaving the Sages to define permitted work.
Mishna: eulogizing and fasting were permitted on the days of slaughter, so as not to support the Sadducees.
Cites an incident at Lod where Rabbi Tarfon barred eulogy for Alexa on Shavuot, which seems to contradict the mishna.
Asks whether the incident could have been on the Festival day itself, since nobody would gather to eulogize then.
Resolves the conflict: Lod concerned a Shavuot whose slaughter day falls on a weekday, while the mishna concerns one falling on Shabbat.

ranges.en: Mishna: hands are washed for non-sacred food, tithes, teruma and sacred food, and immersed for sacred and sin-offering purity.
If the hands become impure, the whole body is impure as well.
Immersing for non-sacred food gives presumptive purity for non-sacred food but forbids tithes.
Immersing for tithes gives presumptive purity for tithes but forbids teruma.
Immersing for teruma gives presumptive purity for teruma but forbids sacred food.
Immersing for sacred food gives presumptive purity for sacred food but forbids contact with purification waters.
Immersing for a stringent category permits eating a lenient one, the principle of the lenient and stringent categories.
Immersion without intending purity counts as no immersion at all.
Mishna: garments of an am ha-aretz, perushim and priests are impure by a zav's treading at successively higher levels of sanctity.
Mishna examples: Yosef ben Yoezer and Yohanan ben Gudgeda, who were extremely careful, nonetheless had garments impure at the higher levels.
Asks whether non-sacred food and tithes actually require hand washing at all.
Cites a Bikkurim mishna that seems to contradict this, since tithes and non-sacred food are said to need no washing.
Restates the two difficulties: tithes against tithes, and non-sacred food against non-sacred food.
Tithes against tithes is resolved by reading the Bikkurim mishna as following Rabbi Meir.
Cites a mishna in Para: the Rabbis treat rabbinic immersion as invalidating tithes, showing tithes differ from non-sacred food.
Frames the remaining difficulty about non-sacred food as still unresolved.
Proposes resolution: the Bikkurim mishna concerns touching alone, while the mishna here concerns eating.
Rav Shimi bar Ashi rejects this: the Rabbis disagree with Rabbi Meir only about eating tithes.
Resolves instead that both mishnayot concern eating, bread requiring washing and fruit not.
Rav Naḥman: one who washes hands for fruit is haughty, since he is more scrupulous than the Sages require.
A baraita: hands washed with intent to purify are pure, and without intent are impure.
Objects that another baraita says the hands are pure whether or not one intended purity.
Rav Naḥman replies that the second baraita refers to non-sacred food, where intent is not required.

ranges.en: The first baraita concerns tithes, where intention to purify oneself is required.
Asks from where we know that non-sacred food does not require intention for purification.
Mikvaot 5:6: a wave of forty se'a falling on a person or vessels leaves them pure, so a person is like vessels without intent.
Objects that the mishna may mean a person sitting and waiting, so the analogy could run the other way.
Asks what the point would be of teaching the sitting-and-waiting case, which is obvious.
Replies the teaching is novel: it rules out decreeing against wave immersion and against edges of waves.
A baraita permits immersion in wave edges but not arches, and Makhshirin 4:7 shows fruit needs no intent for purity.
Rabba objects to Rav Naḥman: the mishna implies intent is needed to take on purity for non-sacred food.
Rav Naḥman replies the mishna only says tithes stay forbidden even when non-sacred purity is taken on.
Rabba objects again: the mishna says one who immersed without intent is as if he never immersed.
Rav Naḥman replies it means no tithes, but non-sacred food is allowed; a baraita confirms this view.
Rabbi Elazar: one who immersed without a definite intent may later assume whatever purity status he wishes.
A baraita objects: one whose foot remains in the water may adjust intent, but once fully out he may not.
Infers from the baraita that a person who has fully ascended may not take on purity at all.
Replies that the baraita means a person in the water may change intent, but once out, intent is fixed.
Asks which Tanna holds that a person with one foot still in the water is still immersing.
Rabbi Pedat cites Mikvaot 7:6, where Rabbi Yehuda holds a foot in the water keeps the immersion ongoing.
Rabba bar Avuh's ruling: the dispute concerns higher Rabbinic purity grades, while passing from impurity to purity is agreed.
An alternative version of Rabba bar Avuh's ruling: the dispute concerns impurity to purity, while higher grades follow Rabbi Yehuda.
Ulla asks Rabbi Yoḥanan how Rabbi Yehuda treats needles on the head of the first immersing person.
Frames the dilemma: does Rabbi Yehuda accept lowering the partition only, or also raising it?
Rabbi Yoḥanan cites a Tosefta where Rabbi Meir allows immersion in the upper pool, which implies raising the partition.
Ulla objects with a baraita in which Rabbi Yehuda seems to dispute this.

ranges.en: Rabbi Meir says immerse in the upper pool, while the other Sage says only in the lower, not the upper one.
Rabbi Yoḥanan replies that if the baraita is taught, it must be accepted, so the Tannaim dispute the matter.
Cites a baraita on one who immersed for non-sacred food and was held to purity for it.
Asks which view the mishna follows, and proposes that the latter clause must be considered.
The latter clause of the mishna, on garments of perushim and teruma eaters, shows a distinction contrary to the Rabbis.
Concludes this supports Rabbi Meir, who holds non-sacred food and tithes are alike.
Asks whether the first clause is the Rabbis' view and the last clause Rabbi Meir's.
Yes: the first clause is the Rabbis' view and the last is Rabbi Meir's, though this is unusual.
Rav Aḥa bar Adda counts five levels in the last clause and reads the whole mishna as the Rabbis' view.
Rav Mari: the mishna shows non-sacred food prepared to sacred standards is treated like sacred food.
Asks from where this inference is derived.

ranges.en: Infers from the fact that the mishna teaches no higher standard for these foods that a distinct level is not recognized.
Asks whether the silence may instead mean these foods are classed with teruma or with non-sacred food, both already taught.
Baraita: non-sacred food prepared to sacred purity standards is like non-sacred food, but Rabbi Elazar son of Tzadok says like teruma.
The last clause of the mishna: Yosei ben Yo'ezer and Yoḥanan ben Gudgeda show the sacred-purity standard for non-sacred food.
Concludes that Yoḥanan ben Gudgeda held such non-sacred food is like sacred food.
Rabbi Yonatan ben Elazar and Rabbi Yonatan ben Amram: a garment is impure if its wearer is distracted when it is exchanged or handed over.
Rabbi Elazar bar Tzadok reports an incident of two women whose clothes were switched in a bathhouse, and Rabbi Akiva ruled them impure.
Rabbi Oshaya objects: by the same logic, a loaf taken from a basket that turns out to be barley would also be impure.
A baraita: one guarding a barrel thought to hold wine that turns out to hold oil leaves it pure from impurity.
Asks: by your reasoning, why does the baraita say the contents may not be eaten?
Rabbi Yirmeya: the baraita refers to one who guarded against impurity that renders others impure, but not against invalidating impurity.
Asks whether one can guard an object only partially, against some types of impurity.
Yes.
A baraita: a hand-in-basket case where the basket is pure and the shovel inside it is impure, since his mind was on the basket only.
Asks why the basket stays pure if the impure shovel could render it impure.
A vessel cannot render another vessel impure, so the basket stays pure.
Asks why the shovel does not then render the food in the basket impure.
Ravina: the baraita refers to one who guarded the shovel from impurity that renders others impure, not from invalidating impurity.
States that the explanation is still difficult, since the barrel's oil should still be impure.
Rabba bar Avuh objects with an incident: a woman's garment was rendered impure when a menstruant pulled its rope.
Rabbi Yishmael replies that the Sages rightly ruled a garment pure only when the mind is focused on guarding it.
A second incident: a woman's thread was tied with her mouth, making the cloth susceptible to impurity through moist contact.
Rabbi Yishmael repeats that focused attention keeps an item pure, and unfocused attention lets it become impure.
Explains the cases: each woman assumes the other is an am ha'aretz, so distraction explains why the garments became impure.
Asks how Rabbi Yonatan ben Elazar's case, where another person holds the shawl, can count as distraction.
Rabbi Yoḥanan: there is a presumption that a person does not guard what is in another's hand.
Asks whether one indeed cannot guard an item held by another.

ranges.en: Baraita: a man's pure food stays pure while his am ha'aretz workers carry it out of sight, but not once they are beyond his sight.
Asks what distinguishes the first clause, where food stays pure, from the latter clause, where it becomes impure.
Rabbi Yitzhak Nappaha: in the first clause the employer had the workers purify themselves beforehand, removing concern for impurity.
Objects that the latter clause should then also be pure.
Am ha'aretz are not careful about contact with others, so the workers may have met another who touched the produce.
Counters that the first clause should then also carry the risk of meeting another am ha'aretz.
The first clause involves a circuitous path, so the workers cannot always see the employer and stay careful.
Asks whether the latter clause should also be cautious, since the employer may appear from around a corner.
The workers rely on the employer's instruction to go ahead, so they do not feel watched and are not careful.
Closing formula of the chapter: Ha-dran alach, Ein doresin.
Mishna: sacred food is stricter than teruma, since vessels may be immersed inside one another only for teruma.
Mishna: one carrying a zav-trodden object may carry teruma but not sacred food.
Mishna: garments of teruma eaters convey zav-trodden impurity to sacred food, unlike teruma.
Mishna: sacred garments and vessels must be untied, dried and immersed before retying, but teruma garments may be retied first.
Mishna: vessels made in purity need immersion for sacred food but not teruma, and sacred food combines contents while teruma does not.
Mishna: fourth-degree impurity disqualifies sacred food, and an impure hand makes its counterpart impure for sacred food but not teruma.
Mishna: sacred food's impure hand conveys impurity to the other hand, and dry foods may be eaten with impure hands only for teruma.

ranges.en: A mourner on the day of death and one still lacking atonement must immerse to eat sacred food, but not for teruma.
Asks why vessels may not be immersed one inside another for sacred food.
Rabbi Ila: the weight of the inner vessel acts as an interposition that keeps water from reaching the contact point.
Objects that the mishna's latter clause shows the concern is interposition, so the first clause must have a different reason.
Quotes the mishna's latter clause on tied garments and vessels, showing sacred food is stricter on interposition.
Both clauses concern interposition; each needed teaching, since each alone would suggest a different reason for the sacred rule.
