ranges.en: Both cases must be taught: knots tighten in water and so create an interposition, while vessels nested in water do not.
Introduces Rabbi Ila's consistent method, citing Rabbi Ila in the name of Rabbi Ḥanina bar Pappa.
Rabbi Ila's count: ten stringencies, with the first five applying to sacred food and sacred-standard non-sacred food, and the last five only to sacred food.
Asks what the reason is for this distinction.
Rabbi Ila explains: the first five have a link to Torah impurity and were extended, while the last five are rabbinic and were not.
Rava disagrees with Rabbi Ila: the first-clause rule is a decree against immersing small items in a narrow-mouthed vessel.

22a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Explains the required opening between water bodies: wide enough for two fingers to twist inside it.
Rava follows Rav Naḥman's teaching in Rabba bar Avuh's name: eleven stringencies, with the last five applying only to sacred food.
Asks what practical difference separates Rava's view from Rabbi Ila's view on nested vessels.
The difference shows with baskets: Rabbi Ila sees interposition, while Rava sees a decree about narrow-mouthed vessels, which baskets lack.
Rava applies his view: baskets of small vessels immersed together are fully pure, even for sacred food.
Rava adds that a basket dividing a ritual bath does not join its two parts, since forty se'a must be in one place.
The rule on nested vessels applies only to pure outer vessels; an impure outer vessel's immersion covers the inner ones too.
Mikvaot 6:2 is cited on nested vessels and joined waters, and its second clause is clarified.
A baraita shows the Rava versus Rabbi Ila dispute is a Tannaitic one, with Abba Shaul agreeing with Rabbi Ila.
Asks whether the teruma case should also be forbidden, given the same two reasons.
The rule against nesting applies to haverim, who know the purity laws, so it is not needed for teruma.
Counters: the same reasoning would apply to sacred food, so why were these concerns extended to it?
Concern: an am ha'aretz may see a haver immersing nested vessels and imitate him without the same precautions.
Objects that the same concern applies to teruma, since an am ha'aretz may imitate a haver there too.
Teruma is not accepted from amei ha'aretz, so their improper immersion does not matter for teruma.
Asks whether sacred food should likewise not be accepted from them.
Refusing sacred food would cause the am ha'aretz resentment and internal discord among Israel.
Asks why the same resentment concern does not apply to teruma.
An am ha'aretz can give his teruma to a friend who is an am ha'aretz priest, but there is only one Temple for sacred food.
Asks which Tanna is concerned about resentment among amei ha'aretz.
A baraita of Rabbi Yosei: wine and oil from amei ha'aretz are accepted so that people do not build private altaras.
Rav Pappa: nowadays testimony from an am ha'aretz is accepted according to Rabbi Yosei's view.
Asks whether we should then worry about borrowing vessels from amei ha'aretz for teruma.
Eduyyot 1:14: Beit Hillel hold an am ha'aretz earthenware vessel shields all impurity, while Beit Shammai limit it to food and drink.
The dispute continues: Beit Shammai hold an am ha'aretz vessel is impure, while Beit Hillel note its contents are declared pure.

22b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: The earlier ruling holds that the am ha'aretz's vessels are pure for him alone, not for haverim, who never treat his items as pure.
A baraita: Rabbi Yehoshua calls Beit Shammai's view illogical, citing a case of an impure metal bowl and pitcher upstairs.
A student of Beit Shammai explains their reasoning: an impure vessel does not serve as a barrier to corpse impurity, per Rabbi Yehoshua.
Asks whether an am ha'aretz's vessel is pure or impure.
It is impure.
The student adds that an am ha'aretz will not heed a claim that his vessel is impure, and will insist on his own purity.
Rabbi Yehoshua prostrates at Beit Shammai's graves and apologizes, and his teeth darkened from his fasts.
Returns to the main point: haverim may borrow am ha'aretz vessels and immerse them before use.
Asks why Beit Hillel did not simply answer that borrowed vessels are immersed before use.
The Gemara explains that immersion helps only with other impurities, while corpse impurity requires sprinkling over seven days.
Objects: a baraita says am ha'aretz are trusted to attest immersion for corpse impurity, contrary to this view.
Abaye: the baraita refers to an am ha'aretz's own body, while the Gemara's ruling refers to his vessels.
Rava: both refer to vessels, and the am ha'aretz is trusted only if he claims he never nested vessels, not otherwise.
A baraita: an am ha'aretz is trusted that produce was not made susceptible, but not that it was made susceptible and not impure.
Objects to Abaye: a baraita says an am ha'aretz is not trusted on his own purity before sprinkling is done.
Abaye revises: the am ha'aretz is held to a strict start, so he may be trusted at the end of the seven days.
Mishna: the rules on the back and inside of a vessel apply to teruma but not to sacred food.
Asks what the back and inside of a vessel means.
Explains from Keilim 25:6: when the back is defiled, only that part is impure; the inside remains pure for teruma but not for sacred food.
Asks what the place for gripping means.
Shmuel explains it as the grip for passing the vessel, and Rabbi Asi as the spot used for dipping.
Rav Beivai's baraita: there is no back-inside difference for vessels of Temple sacred food or outlying sacred food.
Rav Naḥman asks what outlying sacred food means, since teruma is the usual sense.
Rav Naḥman cites the mishna, which applies the back-inside rule to teruma, to argue against that reading.
Suggests the baraita means non-sacred food prepared to sacred purity standards, which is why the phrase outlying fits.
Rabba bar Avuh's teaching of eleven stringencies supports reading the baraita as covering non-sacred food.
Mishna: one carrying a zav-trodden object may carry teruma but not sacred food.
Asks why sacred food is excluded from this allowance.
Rav Yehuda, citing Shmuel, says an incident of moving a barrel of sacred wine led to the enactment.

23a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: The incident of a sandal strap impure from a zav and a barrel: the Sages then decreed that one may carry teruma with an impure object, but not sacred food.
Asks why, if the incident led to a decree, teruma was not also covered by the same decree.
Rabbi Hananya ben Akavya holds decrees are limited to the precise circumstances of the incident that prompted them.
A baraita states the decree on carrying water of purification across the Jordan, and Rabbi Hananya's narrower limit.
Asks what the incident was that gave rise to the decree.
Rav Yehuda, citing Rav, describes the incident: an olive-bulk of corpse matter stuck in a boat's floor during the Jordan crossing.
Raises dilemmas: does the decree cover a pure sandal, a closed barrel, and what is the status of an act transgressing the decree?
Rabbi Ila holds transgressors render the sacred food impure; Rabbi Zeira holds it remains pure.
Asks who completed the vessels made in purity, since a haver's completion would not need immersion.
Concludes the vessels must have been completed by an am ha'aretz, since a haver would not need immersion.
Asks how such vessels can be called completed in purity if an am ha'aretz touch renders them impure.
Shmuel, via Rav Mattana: a haver completed them, but spittle from an am ha'aretz may have fallen on them, so immersion is required.
Asks when the spittle fell: before completion it was not yet a vessel, and after completion the haver would have guarded it.
The spittle fell before completion, and may have stayed moist when the haver finished, so the vessel needs immersion.
The mishna implies immersion suffices, without waiting for sunset, for such vessels.
Para 5:4: Rabbi Eliezer says a reed tube should be immersed at once, while Rabbi Yehoshua says it must first be rendered impure.
Asks who cut the tube, since a haver cutting it would not need immersion.
Asks whether, if an am ha'aretz cut it, Rabbi Yehoshua would require first rendering it impure, since it is already impure.
Rav Mattana citing Shmuel: a haver cut it, and immersion is required because am ha'aretz spittle may have touched it.
Asks when the spittle fell: before cutting it is not a vessel, and afterward the haver would have guarded it.
The spittle fell before cutting, and may have remained moist when the haver finished, so immersion is needed.
For Rabbi Yehoshua, the rule creates a visible rejection of the Sadducees.
Para 3:7: priests who burned the red heifer were rendered impure on purpose to refute the Sadducees' sunset requirement.
Asks what demonstration against the Sadducees Rabbi Eliezer's view can offer if immersion alone suffices.
Rav: Rabbi Eliezer does not require sunset for vessels completed in purity, yet a demonstrative sign still rejects the Sadducees.

23b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: They treated the red heifer tube as impure like a dead creeping animal, which makes the sun-setting rule unnecessary.
Objects: an item impure from a creeping animal would not render people impure, yet a baraita says the cutter must immerse.
A baraita: one who cuts and immerses the tube must immerse, so the tube does render people impure.
Objects: if it is like a corpse impurity, it would also need sprinkling on the third and seventh days.
The same baraita says immersion is required but not sprinkling on the third and seventh days.
The tube is treated as impure from a corpse on its seventh day, after sprinkling, so it needs only immersion.
Objects: a baraita says the Sages never innovated new impurity rules for the red heifer, which this tube treatment would be.
Abaye: the no-innovation rule means a spade on which a zav sits does not become impure as a seat, citing Leviticus 15:6.
The baraita continues: the seat rule applies only to objects designed for sitting, so the red heifer vessels are excluded.
Mishna: a vessel combines its contents for sacred food but not for teruma.
Asks from where this rule that a vessel combines its contents is derived.
Rabbi Ḥanin cites Numbers 7:14, one pan of ten shekels full of incense, to show the vessel's contents act as one.
Rav Kahana objects with Eduyyot 8:1, where Rabbi Akiva adds flour, incense and coals as items combined in one vessel.
Asks whether the combining rule for these items is only rabbinic, and how we know that.
The first clause of the mishna records Rabbi Shimon ben Beteira's ruling on ashes, and Rabbi Akiva's addition follows it.
Reish Lakish cites Bar Kappara on a further point about combined contents.

24a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Rabbi Akiva's testimony covers only rabbinic-law combining; by Torah law a vessel combines only items that need one, such as the meal-offering remainder.
Asks what can be said for incense and frankincense, which clearly need a vessel, if flour was the only item where combining is rabbinic.
Rav Nahman, citing Rabba bar Avuh, explains the case is piling them on a flat leather board, which has no inside, so combining is only rabbinic.
Rabbi Hanin's view that combining is Torah law conflicts with Rabbi Hiyya bar Abba's report of Rabbi Yohanan that the mishna rests on Akiva's testimony.
Quotes the mishna itself: an item of the fourth degree of impurity disqualifies sacrificial food.
A baraita is introduced, giving the teaching of Rabbi Yosei.
Asks from where we know that the fourth degree of impurity disqualifies sacrificial food.
A fortiori argument: one lacking atonement is disqualified for sacred food, so an item impure to the third degree should make sacred food fourth-degree impure.
Asks from where the Torah-law third degree of impurity for sacred food is derived.
Cites the verse in Leviticus 7:19 that meat touching any impure thing shall not be eaten.
Explains the verse covers meat touched by a second-degree impurity, so the third degree is from the Torah and the fourth follows a fortiori.
The mishna contrasts teruma with sacred food: an impure hand makes the other impure only for sacred food.
Rav Sheizevi limits the hand rule to cases where the pure hand touches sacred food while the impure hand does.
Abaye objects with a baraita that a dry impure hand also makes the other impure, arguing Rav Sheizevi's limit makes the teaching pointless.
Reish Lakish limits the rule: the impure hand affects the other only when both hands belong to the same person.

24b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Continues the earlier view: an impure hand does not render the other hand impure.
Rabbi Yohanan holds an impure hand disqualifies food through the other hand, own or another's, but does not render it impure.
Asks from where Rabbi Yohanan derives this, since the latter clause of the mishna repeats what the first clause already taught.
Concludes the repetition must add the other hand, so the rule covers another person's hand too.
Reish Lakish retracts and agrees with Rabbi Yohanan: an impure hand disqualifies, whether its own or another's, but does not render impure.
Notes this is a tannaitic dispute and quotes the mishna: Rabbi Yehoshua says a hand renders the other impure, while the Rabbis disagree.
Asks whether the Rabbis' reply implies the second hand only disqualifies food by fourth-degree impurity, not by third-degree impurity.
Rejects that inference: perhaps the Rabbis deny one impure hand affects the other at all, and the mishna follows Rabbi Yehoshua.
Rather, the dispute is like the tannaitic disagreement in the baraita over how much impurity one hand imparts to the other.
The baraita: a dry impure hand renders the other impure for sacred food but not teruma, per Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi; Rabbi Yosei son of Rabbi Yehuda disagrees.
Quotes the mishna: one may eat dry foods with impure hands for teruma, but not for sacred food.
Rabbi Hanina ben Antigonus asks whether dry food can exist for sacred food, since sanctity itself makes it susceptible to impurity.
The case is food placed in his mouth by another, or moved with a spindle, while he eats ordinary radish or onion; the decree applies to sacred food only.
Quotes the mishna: an acute mourner and one lacking atonement must immerse before eating sacred food, but not for teruma.
Asks what the reason is for requiring immersion for these people before eating sacred food.
Because until now they were forbidden to eat sacred food, they may not have guarded against impurity, so the Sages required immersion.
Mishna: in Judea people are trusted about the purity of wine and oil all year, and during press season also for teruma.
Mishna continued: after press season a priest may not take teruma wine from amei ha'aretz, but may accept it next season; sacred claim is trusted.

25a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Mishna: amei ha'aretz are trusted about certain wine and oil during press season and seventy days before it, in Judea but not in the Galilee.
Asks what the reason is for the difference between Judea and the Galilee.
Reish Lakish: a strip of Samaritan territory separates the two regions, so Galilean produce would become impure on the way to Judea.
Objects that the Galileans could carry the wine and oil in a closed box, chest or closet, which would protect it from impurity.
Identifies the view as Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi's, who holds a moving tent is not a tent, and cites a baraita on entering gentile lands in a box.
Objects that the oil and wine could be carried in a sealed earthenware vessel, which would protect it from impurity.
Rabbi Eliezer's baraita: sacred food is not spared from impurity by being in a vessel with a tightly bound cover.
Objects with a baraita that the red-heifer water is not spared by a tightly covered vessel, seeming to contradict Rabbi Eliezer's view.
Asks whether the baraita then implies that sacred food is spared in such a vessel.
No: the inference concerns water not yet consecrated with the ashes, which is spared even if designated for that use later.
Objects that Ulla said haverim prepare their wine and oil to the purity standard of sacred food in the Galilee, implying they could transport it.
Indeed they could not transport it; they left it in place, expecting Elijah to purify the road from Galilee to Judea.
Mishna: during the winepress and olive press seasons, amei ha'aretz are trusted even for teruma.
Objects with a baraita: a farmer who finishes pressing leaves a basket of olives for a poor priest, showing amei ha'aretz are not trusted to make pure oil.
Rav Nahman: no contradiction; the mishna refers to those who press early in the season, and the baraita to those who press late.
Rav Adda bar Ahava asks for an example of the late pressers Rav Nahman described.
Rav Nahman's own father's olives, pressed late; Rav Yosef instead says the rule in the baraita refers only to the Galilee.
Abaye objects with a baraita that Transjordan and the Galilee are like Judea, so the Galilee-only resolution fails.
Rather, the original answer stands: the baraita refers to the period after the winepress season has ended.
Mishna: after press season a priest may not accept teruma wine from amei ha'aretz, but the giver may keep it for the next season.
The students ask Rav Sheshet: if a priest accepted such wine anyway, may he himself leave it over for the next season?
Rav Sheshet replies that they learned the answer in a mishna, which he then cites.

25b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Mishna on brothers, a ha'ver and an am ha'aretz, dividing inherited produce: permitted when the items are the same kind, prohibited when they differ.
A baraita: if the share mixes wet and dry produce, the ha'ver burns the wet teruma and may keep the dry.
Asks why the ha'ver must burn the wet teruma rather than leave it until the next winepress season.
The baraita concerns items with no winepress, or that would spoil before the Festival, so the option of waiting does not apply.
Mishna: if the am ha'aretz declares a quarter-log of sacred wine or oil in the barrel he is believed; then the Oholot mishna on examining ground.
Asks what the term examine means in the mishna on examining the ground.
Shmuel: one blows on the ground of a beit haperas while walking through it, so any bone fragments are blown from the path.
Ulla's view, given by Rabbi Hiyya bar Abba: a trodden beit haperas is pure for Passover; teruma is stricter, since eating it while impure is a capital offense.
Raises the dilemma: if one examined the ground for his Passover offering, may he then eat teruma?
Ulla: yes, he is permitted, since he is declared pure for the offering and cannot be impure for teruma.
Rabba bar Ulla: no, it is prohibited for him to eat teruma after such an examination.
An elder cites the mishna on believing the am ha'aretz's quarter-log declaration to support Ulla, reasoning that credibility carries over from sacred food to teruma.
Mishna fragment: jugs of mingled wine and oil, and the sum of wine and oil.
A baraita: amei ha'aretz are not believed about flasks or about teruma.
Asks which flasks are meant; if sacred food, the am ha'aretz is trusted about them, but if teruma, why is he trusted about flasks when not about teruma?
Rather, the flasks are empty sacred ones during the rest of the year, and full teruma flasks during the winepress season.
Asks whether the mishna's mingled jugs refer to teruma mixed in, which would clash with the baraita.
The school of Rabbi Hiyya: it refers to ordinary wine or oil mixed with sacred wine or oil.
Asks whether the term mingled can apply to sacred food at all.
The school of Rabbi Elai: the mishna concerns wine tevel kept for libations, which mixes sacred, teruma and ordinary produce.
Mishna: amei ha'aretz are also believed seventy days before the winepress season.
Abaye derives from this mishna that a tenant farmer must prepare flasks seventy days before the pressing.
Mishna: within Modi'im potters are believed about their earthenware; outside Modi'im they are not, with examples of entering and leaving.
A baraita: Modi'im is sometimes treated as inside the perimeter and sometimes as outside, depending on who is entering or leaving.

26a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Continues the Modi'im mishna: if both potter and ha'ver are leaving the perimeter, they count as outside and the ha'ver may not buy the vessels.
Abaye reads the Modi'im mishna's two clauses together and infers that the case must be one where both parties are entering or both leaving.
A tosefta on small earthenware vessels for sacred use; Reish Lakish and Rabbi Yohanan dispute whether handheld size matters and whether full vessels count.
Rava explains that Rabbi Yohanan agrees liquids inside are impure, since the decree on vessels does not cancel impurity of the liquid, citing a parallel case.
Mishna: tax collectors and thieves who return vessels are believed that they touched nothing else, and in Jerusalem amei ha'aretz are believed about sacred food.
Objects with a mishna in Teharot stating that if tax collectors entered a house, the whole house is impure.
The contradiction is resolved: that mishna concerns a gentile present, while this one concerns none; the Teharot mishna's rules for that case are quoted.
Asks what difference a gentile's presence makes to the halakha.
Rabbi Yohanan and Rabbi Elazar dispute whether the fear is of the gentile himself or of the government.
The practical difference shows up with a gentile who is unimportant: he cannot command them, but could still report them to authorities.
Mishna on thieves who returned the vessels they took, believed as the tax collectors are.
Objects with a Teharot mishna that only the thieves' footprint area is impure, so their claims about other vessels should not be accepted.
Rav Pinhas in Rav's name: the mishna refers to thieves who repented, which the wording about returning vessels implies.
Mishna and a baraita: amei ha'aretz are believed for large and small earthenware for sacred food in Jerusalem, and for teruma at a festival.
Asks why the Sages were so lenient about these vessels.
Because potters' kilns may not be built in Jerusalem, so vessels had to be brought in from outside the city.
Asks from where these rules about festival days derive.
Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi cites Judges 20:11 that when all Israel gathers as one man, the Torah makes them all ha'verim.
Mishna: one who opened his wine barrel or began kneading dough on the festival may finish selling it after; Rabbi Yehuda permits, the Sages forbid.
Rabbi Ami and Rabbi Yitzhak Nappaha ask whether one may leave the wine for another festival and then sell it in purity.
Objects that everyone's hands touch the wine, so leaving it for another festival cannot even be considered.
Replies that until now everyone's touch was permitted during the festival, showing that such contact did not render it impure.
Rejoins that the festival is different: the Merciful One declared the touch pure only during the festival, while afterward it is impure again.
Suggests the amoraic dispute mirrors a tannaitic dispute between two baraitot, one allowing and one forbidding leaving it for another festival.
Rejects that suggestion: one baraita may follow Rabbi Yehuda's view that the wine can be finished after the festival, the other the Sages' view.
Objects that Rabbi Yehuda himself permits finishing the wine after the festival, so the baraitot cannot be read that way.
Resolves it: the baraita forbidding leaving follows Rabbi Yehuda, since he has no need to leave it and may finish selling immediately.
Mishna: vessels of the Temple courtyard are purified after the festival, with Rabbi Yehuda's view on a Thursday ending.
A baraita explains Rabbi Yehuda's reason: the priests are busy removing the large quantity of ash after the festival.
Mishna continues: how the vessels are purified, immersing those used in the Temple and warning the amei ha'aretz priests to be careful.

26b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Mishna: the Temple vessels had spare substitutes and needed immersion after the festival, except the golden and bronze altars, per Rabbi Eliezer, since they are like ground or coated.
A baraita warns the am ha'aretz priests not to touch the table or the candelabrum.
Asks why our mishna does not also mention the candelabrum, as the baraita does.
The table's verse says shewbread before Me always, which the candelabrum's verse lacks, so only the table must stay in place.
The other tanna argues the verse about setting the candelabrum opposite the table makes it permanent too, which the mishna's tanna denies.
Proposes deriving that the table cannot become impure, since a large wooden vessel designed to rest in place is not susceptible to impurity.
Asks what the reason is for the wooden-vessel rule.
Wooden vessels must be carried both full and empty, like a sack, to be susceptible, and the table is carried too, per Reish Lakish.
Reish Lakish cites Leviticus 24:6, 'upon the pure table', to show the table is capable of impurity.
Asks why the table is susceptible to impurity at all if it is a fixed wooden vessel.
The table is lifted to show the shewbread to pilgrims, and the shewbread stayed as hot as when placed, a great miracle cited from Samuel.
Proposes that the table is impure because of its gold coating, citing the Kelim mishna that a wooden table fully coated in stone is not susceptible.
Suggests acacia wood is valuable and not nullified by coating, which works for Reish Lakish's view on expensive masmi wood.
Rabbi Yohanan holds even expensive vessels are nullified by coating, so this answer fails for him.
Suggests the gold on the table is fixed in one case and not fixed in the Kelim case, distinguishing the two.
Reish Lakish asks Rabbi Yohanan whether the coating rule applies only to fixed coatings and only to coatings covering the rim.
Rabbi Yohanan says fixedness and rim coverage make no difference, so the table needs a different explanation: the table is special.

27a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Ezekiel 41:22 calls the table wood, so its wooden identity survives the gold coating and it is impure only if carried out to pilgrims.
Rabbi Yohanan and Reish Lakish: while the Temple stands the altar atones; now a person's table atones, since feeding guests atones. Then the mishna on substitute vessels is restated.
Exodus 20:21 and Numbers 3:31 show the bronze and golden altars are both like the ground, since the plural altars are compared.
The mishna's Rabbis say the altars are impure-exempt because they are coated, which is the reason the mishna gives.
Objects that coating should make the altars impure, since a metal-coated item is a metal vessel.
Proposes emending the mishna so the Rabbis disagree with Rabbi Eliezer entirely and hold the altars susceptible because coated.
Alternatively the Rabbis answer Rabbi Eliezer: the coating is nullified, so they are simply wooden vessels fixed in place.
Rabbi Abbahu cites Rabbi Elazar: the fire of Gehenna has no power over Torah scholars.
A fortiori from the salamander, which resists fire, and from Jeremiah 23:29, that Torah words, like fire, become part of the scholars' bodies.
Reish Lakish: the fire of Gehenna has no power over the sinners of Israel either.
A fortiori from the golden altar, which fire does not harm; Song of Songs 4:3 is read as reikanin, so the empty sinners are full of good deeds.
Closing formula for the chapter Hamedir Bakodesh and the tractate Chagigah.
